name: The Last Prayer
summary: A teaching preserved across generations of the Omnia faith — of those who sought communion with the goddess and were never seen again, and the parable told in the temples to explain why.
body:
### The Parable of the Old Tree

There is a story told in the temples — old enough that no one remembers its source.

A boy lived across from an old tree. He was a good climber, light and quick, and the tree tempted him. His father took him aside one evening and told him plainly: *never climb that tree. The branches are old. They will break under you.* The boy heard his father. He also heard the tree.

He climbed it anyway — a dozen times, two dozen, throughout the years of his childhood. The branches held. They always held. And so, in his mind, the warning aged into foolishness. His father had simply been wrong.

Decades passed. The boy became a man. He had a son of his own, and one afternoon he told the story — not as a cautionary tale, but as evidence. *My father warned me,* he said, *but I knew better, and nothing ever happened.* He wanted to prove it. He crossed the yard and climbed the tree again, the way he had climbed it a hundred times before, and settled his weight onto one of the lower branches.

The branch did not consider his history. It broke. He fell.

The priests tell this story not to speak of trees, but of Omnia.

### The Last Prayer

It is known — recorded across generations in the quieter annals of the faith — that monks and priests who attempt to pray in direct communion with Omnia do not simply die.

They disappear. Completely. No body is recovered. No trace persists. Not even the particular quality of their absence lingers, the way a room sometimes holds the shape of someone who has left it. After the prayer, there is nothing where they were. It is as though they never occupied that space at all.

This does not happen to everyone who prays. The faith is careful on this point. It happens only to those who have climbed high enough — the most spiritually refined, the most genuinely devout, those whose practice has made them transparent enough to actually evoke the presence of the goddess rather than merely speak in her direction. The ordinary worshipper is safe in their distance. It is only those who draw close enough to be truly seen who vanish.

Every generation produces at least one who believes they will be different. They have climbed the tree a hundred times. The branches always held. They are ready, they are pure, they are certain. They make the prayer.

None of them return.

Others have been taken by simpler things — curiosity, mostly, or the particular pride of the scholarly. They had no great devotion. They simply wanted to know what was on the other side. They received their answer in full, and were not there afterward to share it.

What awaits beyond the prayer, no living person can say with authority. There are three accounts preserved across the traditions.

The first holds that what is called vanishing is not death at all, but the eternal and ecstatic embrace of the goddess — that those who disappear are not destroyed but *received*, gathered entirely into the totality of Omnia, which is to say, into everything. In this reading, the prayer is not an ending but a completion, and those who have made it are the only ones who have ever truly arrived anywhere.

The second holds that the dissolution of the one who prays is a punishment — a correction, swift and absolute, for the insolence of imagining oneself close enough to Omnia to address her directly. That she is not deaf to these prayers. That she hears them precisely. And that the silence that follows is her only reply.

The third account offers no moral and asks for none: perhaps it is simply what happens when something finite touches something infinite. Perhaps there is no intent behind it at all — no embrace, no punishment, only consequence. A moth does not offend the flame.

No one who has made the leap of faith has returned to tell us which of these is true. This, perhaps, is the most honest thing about Omnia: the question she raises most clearly is the one she will never allow to be answered.
